what_its_for: Rifaximin is an antibiotic used to treat traveler's diarrhea caused by certain bacteria (E. coli). It is also used to reduce the chance of a serious brain condition called hepatic encephalopathy (HE) coming back in adults with liver disease. Some doctors also prescribe it for irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea (IBS-D).
how_to_take: Swallow the tablet whole with or without food. Do not crush, chew, or break the tablet. Take it at the same times each day to help you remember. Finish all of your medication even if you start feeling better, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
dosing: The dose depends on what condition is being treated. For traveler's diarrhea: usually 200 mg three times a day for 3 days. For preventing hepatic encephalopathy: usually 550 mg twice a day, taken long-term. For IBS-D: usually 550 mg three times a day for 14 days. Always follow the exact dose your doctor prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Keep this medicine out of reach of children. Do not use after the expiration date printed on the package.
what_to_avoid: Do not use rifaximin if you have bloody diarrhea or a fever, as these may be signs of a more serious infection that needs a different antibiotic. Avoid taking it if you have a known allergy to rifaximin or similar antibiotics like rifampin or rifabutin. Tell your doctor about all medicines you are taking, as rifaximin may interact with blood thinners like warfarin. Avoid alcohol while taking this medication.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you develop: bloody or worsening diarrhea, high fever, severe stomach pain or cramping, signs of an allergic reaction (skin rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, difficulty breathing), yellowing of the skin or eyes, or if your symptoms do not improve within 24 to 48 hours of starting treatment for traveler's diarrhea. Also call if you notice unusual bruising or bleeding, which could be a sign of a drug interaction.
when_it_works: For traveler's diarrhea, you may start to feel better within 24 to 48 hours. For hepatic encephalopathy prevention, this medicine works over the long term to help keep episodes from coming back, so it may take time to see the full benefit. For IBS-D, some improvement may be noticed during the 14-day treatment course.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before using this medicine if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, as the safety has not been fully established. Children: The safety and effectiveness in children under 12 years of age has not been established. Elderly patients: No special dose adjustment is needed for older adults, but they should be monitored closely. Liver disease patients: Use with caution and only under close doctor supervision. Kidney disease patients: No dose adjustment is typically needed, but inform your doctor of any kidney problems.
